What does this step demonstrate?
  1. Preserve company/year provenance; check duplicate, misassigned and ambiguous-version texts.
  2. Normalize the text, remove stopwords and explicit management/reporting boilerplate, and retain business words and phrases.
  3. Compare frequency and TF-IDF with a shared vocabulary and IDF across the joint study corpus.
  4. Explore distributions with clouds, then verify changes against numeric weights and source passages.

Cleaning rules and known limitations

Across the original 2020 file, 1,506 rows shared normalized text with another company. Affected study records were conservatively excluded. Different versions within one company/year were not concatenated when their relationship could not be established.

Deduplication does not authenticate identity. Nine subsequently confirmed mismatches are excluded from this experiment, leaving 661 firms and 1,322 texts. Review flags remain visible; an automated screen is not verification.

TF-IDF and Word2Vec use the same joint-year study corpus for retrospective comparison. Cosine scores are not confidence estimates, and higher embedding scores do not establish better relevance.

Candidates are restricted to the same year and subgroup. Word overlap can reflect products, customers, partners, suppliers, regulation or patents. Reading judgments separate specific business-line support, ecosystem links and weak matches.

Extracts are exact substrings of supplied CSV texts and may retain encoding artifacts or incomplete sentences. Source rows and character ranges are zero-based. The files lack independently verified filing accessions and dates.
